grammar_points.name: 〜みたいに (mitai ni) — like ~

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Noun + みたいに (mitai ni) means "like ~" and is the casual equivalent of のように (no you ni). みたい (mitai) expresses resemblance, and に (ni) turns it into an adverb. Before a noun, use みたいな (mitai na): 夢みたいな話 (yume mitai na hanashi, "a story like a dream"). It sounds more conversational and informal.

Example from this song:
太陽みたいに (taiyou mitai ni) — "like the sun"
The singer compares someone to the sun — warm, bright, and life-giving.

More examples:
• 子供みたいに笑う (kodomo mitai ni warau) — "laugh like a child"
• 映画みたいな恋 (eiga mitai na koi) — "a romance like a movie"
• 夢みたいだ (yume mitai da) — "it's like a dream"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 太陽 (taiyou, "sun") + みたいに (mitai ni) → 太陽みたいに (taiyou mitai ni, "like the sun")

grammar_points.name: 〜続ける (tsuzukeru) — to keep doing

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb ます-stem (masu-stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru) means "to keep doing ~" or "to continue doing ~." It emphasizes persistence and endurance. Combined with ている (te iru): 続けている (tsuzukete iru, "has been continuing"). Casual: 続けてる (tsuzuketeru).

Example from this song:
走り続けてる (hashiri tsuzuketeru) — "keeps running" (casual)
The singer describes someone who never stops running — relentless determination.

More examples:
• 信じ続ける (shinji tsuzukeru) — "keep believing"
• 10年間書き続けている (juu-nenkan kaki tsuzukete iru) — "has been writing for 10 years"
• 歩き続けよう (aruki tsuzukeyou) — "let's keep walking"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 走る (hashiru, "to run") → 走り (hashiri, masu-stem) + 続ける (tsuzukeru) → 走り続ける (hashiri tsuzukeru, "keep running") → 走り続けてる (hashiri tsuzuketeru, casual progressive)

grammar_points.name: 〜なんて (nante) — such a thing as / how surprising that

explanation.en:
How it works:
なんて (nante) expresses surprise, disbelief, or dismissiveness about something. After a verb or noun, it means "such a thing as ~" (often dismissive) or "how ~ !" (expressing surprise). It can belittle something or express amazement depending on context.

Example from this song:
あきらめるなんて (akirameru nante) — "such a thing as giving up"
The singer dismisses the very idea of giving up — it is unthinkable.

More examples:
• 嘘なんて信じない (uso nante shinjinai) — "I don't believe such a thing as lies"
• こんなに美しいなんて (konna ni utsukushii nante) — "how beautiful!"
• 失敗するなんて思わなかった (shippai suru nante omowanakatta) — "I never thought I'd fail"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: あきらめる (akirameru, "to give up") + なんて (nante, "such a thing as") → あきらめるなんて (akirameru nante, "such a thing as giving up")

grammar_points.name: 〜たって (tatte) — even if (casual)

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb た-form (ta-form) + って (tte) is a casual form of ても (temo), meaning "even if ~." It sounds tougher and more defiant. For nouns: なくたって (nakutatte, "even without"). This form is very common in song lyrics and casual speech.

Example from this song:
負けたって (maketatte) — "even if you lose"
なくたって (nakutatte) — "even without"
The singer encourages perseverance regardless of setbacks.

More examples:
• 失敗したって気にしない (shippai shitatte ki ni shinai) — "even if I fail, I don't care"
• 金がなくたって幸せだ (kane ga nakutatte shiawase da) — "even without money, I'm happy"
• 笑われたって構わない (warawaretatte kamawanai) — "I don't mind even if I'm laughed at"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 負ける (makeru, "to lose") → 負けた (maketa, past) + って (tte) → 負けたって (maketatte, "even if you lose")

grammar_points.name: 〜てくる (te kuru) — approaching / coming toward

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + くる (kuru) expresses something coming toward the speaker or the present moment. It can mean: (1) an action approaching — 伝わってくる (tsutawatte kuru, "comes through / reaches me"), (2) a change developing up to now — 暗くなってきた (kuraku natte kita, "it's gotten dark"), (3) going and coming back — 買ってくる (katte kuru, "go buy and come back").

Example from this song:
伝わってくる (tsutawatte kuru) — "comes through / reaches me"
The feelings or message travels toward the singer and arrives.

More examples:
• 雨が降ってきた (ame ga futte kita) — "it started raining" (change approaching now)
• お腹が空いてきた (onaka ga suite kita) — "I'm getting hungry" (gradual change)
• コンビニで買ってくる (konbini de katte kuru) — "I'll go buy it at the convenience store (and come back)"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 伝わる (tsutawaru, "to be transmitted") → 伝わって (tsutawatte, te-form) + くる (kuru, "to come") → 伝わってくる (tsutawatte kuru, "comes through / reaches me")

grammar_points.name: 受身形 (ukemi-kei) — passive form 〜られる/〜れる

explanation.en:
How it works:
The passive form means the subject receives an action. For godan (u-verb) verbs: change -u to -a + れる (reru). For ichidan (ru-verb) verbs: drop る (ru) + られる (rareru). Japanese passive often implies adversity — something unwanted happening to the subject.

Example from this song:
言われる (iwareru) — "to be told"
引き離される (hikihanasareru) — "to be pulled apart"
Both express being on the receiving end of actions imposed by others.

More examples:
• 先生に褒められた (sensei ni homerareta) — "was praised by the teacher"
• 雨に降られた (ame ni furareta) — "got rained on" (adversity)
• 彼に嘘をつかれた (kare ni uso o tsukareta) — "was lied to by him"

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 引き離す (hikishanasu, "to pull apart") → 引き離される (hikihanasareru, passive, "to be pulled apart")
